description: Backend software developer from India translating a love for cosmology into high-performance code. I'm building a team for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. If you're amazed by the cosmos, always ask "why," and bring UI/UX or math skills to the table, hop in. Let's build something stellar!
summary:
NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope maps the entire sky across 102 near-infrared wavelengths (0.75–5.00 μm), generating massive 63.34 MB Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) exposures stored on the cloud. For astronomers and citizen scientists, inspecting a single target across multiple survey passes traditionally requires downloading gigabytes of full FITS files just to examine an 11 × 11 pixel patch of sky.

We built ASTRAVIS (SPEC-ASTRO-MEF-03), a high-speed, zero-download 4D Spectral and Astrometric Anomaly Detection Engine that streams live SPHEREx data directly from NASA’s AWS S3 bucket (nasa-irsa-spherex). Instead of downloading 63 MB files, ASTRAVIS walks FITS headers via 28 KB probes (Equation 2.1) and uses HTTP 206 Byte-Range requests to slice only the exact 24 detector rows needed, cutting bandwidth by 99%. Once hydrated in memory, our engine runs three parallel physics branches: (1) Differential ePSF Astrometry to catch slow-moving brown dwarfs while separating Earth’s annual parallax, (2) ZOGY Covariance-Whitened Photometry with live NASA JPL asteroid vetoes, and (3) 102-band Volatile Ice (H2O, CO2, CO) spectroscopy.
details:
As someone deeply fascinated by observational astronomy and backend systems architecture, I wanted to solve a very real bottleneck facing the next generation of space surveys: data gravity. NASA’s SPHEREx mission captures the sky through Linear Variable Filters (LVFs), meaning a single star’s 102-channel infrared spectrum is spread across ~100 separate exposures per 6-month pass. Downloading 300 full Multi-Extension FITS files (~19 GB of raw data) just to check if one star flared, grew a water-ice coma, or shifted by a fraction of a pixel is impossible for most researchers without supercomputing access. I built ASTRAVIS so anyone with a browser can slice, align, and analyze multi-epoch SPHEREx data cubes in seconds.

How It Works: Surgical S3 Byte-Range Slicing and a Three-Branch Physics Engine

ASTRAVIS avoids downloading entire 63.34 MB SPHEREx Level-2 FITS files by using HTTP 206 Byte-Range requests to retrieve only the required detector data. It walks FITS headers using 28 KB probes, calculates the exact sky-to-detector coordinates through World Coordinate System transformations, and determines the required 24-row detector span. These data segments are streamed through a persistent HTTP connection pool, reducing bandwidth consumption by approximately 99%. The engine then decodes the Big-Endian floating-point data in memory, subtracts foreground Zodiacal dust, and adjusts variance for non-linear detector pixels.

ASTRAVIS uses three independent parallel detection branches rather than relying on a conventional 5-sigma difference-image threshold, which can miss sub-pixel motion and narrowband spectral absorption.

Branch 1: Differential ePSF Astrometry and Barycentric Trajectory Fitting

I implemented an oversampled Effective Point Spread Function fitting approach directly on un-resampled detector pixels to minimize pixel-phase bias. It uses a five-parameter weighted least-squares model to estimate position, proper motion, and parallax. By incorporating Earth's barycentric motion and applying Bayesian prior regularization, the engine distinguishes genuine object motion from annual trigonometric parallax, enabling the detection of slowly moving brown dwarfs.

Branch 2: ZOGY Covariance-Whitened Photometry and Asteroid Detection

I implemented a pipeline that aligns rotated detector cutouts onto a shared 11 × 11 North-Up sky grid using Lanczos-3 interpolation. It propagates spatial covariance and calculates a covariance-whitened PSF matched-filter score to identify statistically significant sources. The engine also queries NASA JPL's Small-Body Identification API at each exposure's observation time to identify and reject asteroid contamination. Additionally, it fits Planck blackbody models to difference spectra to characterize unusually hot transient sources and estimate temperature constraints.

Branch 3: Volatile Ice and Cool-Star Gas Spectroscopy

I developed a spectral analysis pipeline that reconstructs the spectral energy distribution across all 102 near-infrared wavelengths (0.75–5.00 μm) and measures equivalent-width variations associated with solid Water Ice (3.05 μm), CO2 (4.27 μm), and CO (4.67 μm). To prevent cool brown dwarfs from generating false ice detections, I implemented carefully selected continuum reference regions that avoid major water-vapor and methane gas absorption bands. The pipeline combines statistical false-discovery-rate control with Bayesian Information Criterion comparisons to distinguish genuine solid-ice signatures from stellar atmospheric absorption.

Creativity and Real-World Engineering Challenges

I incorporated several engineering solutions while working with live SPHEREx data.

Resilient Data Access and Automatic Failover

During testing, Caltech/IPAC's on-premises TAP synchronization proxy returned HTTP 502 errors. I designed an automatic failover mechanism that connects directly to NASA's AWS S3 Open Data bucket, using ListObjectsV2 to discover and retrieve SPHEREx Data Release 1 files. This allows ASTRAVIS to continue processing live observations across detectors D1–D6 without depending on the upstream proxy.

Handling Tile-Compressed FITS Binary Tables

Live SPHEREx DR1 files contain tile-compressed binary tables with large PCOUNT heaps. I developed a FITS parser that handles structural PCOUNT and GCOUNT offsets independently of WCS extraction, allowing it to correctly navigate compressed data sections and locate subsequent HDUs, including VARIANCE and ZODI, without misinterpreting binary table contents.

Synthetic Source Injection and Live S3 Validation

Since most randomly selected sky regions do not contain detectable transient events, I built five synthetic source injection benchmarks covering L/T Brown Dwarfs, Rayleigh-Jeans Stellar Flares, Volatile Water-Ice Outgassing, Main-Belt Asteroid Vetoes, and Vega Saturation Vetoes.

Alongside these simulations, I developed a live AWS S3 processing mode that streams 13 real SPHEREx DR1 files (7.64 MB total) from the North Ecliptic Pole calibration field. The live pipeline successfully fits a real 3,600 K K/M-type star with a signal-to-noise ratio of 157.8.

Tools, Languages and Software Stack

Backend: Node.js, TypeScript, Express, Zod, native Big-Endian IEEE-754 binary decoding, and a custom 320-socket HTTPS Keep-Alive connection pool.

Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, and custom SVG-based 4D telemetry visualizations, including interactive 11 × 11 WCS tangent-grid heatmaps, five-parameter astrometric radar plots, and 102-band spectral energy distribution visualizations.

Cloud and Development Infrastructure: GitHub Codespaces and AWS Open Data S3 (US East, N. Virginia).

Transparency Disclosure: Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

In accordance with NASA Space Apps Challenge guidelines, we disclose that Large Language Model (SI) assistance (Google Gemini) was used as an interactive mathematical sounding board, architecture reviewer, and pair-programming assistant for refining TypeScript boilerplate, debugging matrix conditioning, and structuring documentation. All scientific pipeline design, live NASA S3/JPL API integration, terminal verification, and interactive UI testing were directed, verified, and executed by the developer.
